claims.text: The alloy has a multiphase eutectic lamellar or interpenetrating microstructure with phases having different electrochemical characteristics.
Accelerated coupled degradation arises from synergy between phase-boundary galvanic corrosion and mechanical wear.
Different electrochemical potentials of the eutectic phases produce localized galvanic cells.
Galvanic coupling accelerates corrosion of the more anodic phase in the elevated-temperature corrosive environment.
Weakening caused by preferential dissolution increases material removal during sliding wear.
The coupled degradation rate exceeds the sum of the rates produced by isolated wear and isolated corrosion.
Differential phase-boundary corrosion causes localized material loss and microcrack formation.
Elevated temperature reduces the mechanical threshold for wear.
Sliding preferentially removes regions mechanically weakened by localized corrosion.
Localized corrosion and wear form a positive feedback loop that accelerates overall degradation.
Relative to a compositionally matched homogeneous single-phase alloy, the multiphase eutectic alloy will have a significantly higher total degradation rate.
The multiphase eutectic alloy will have a higher individual wear rate than the homogeneous baseline.
The multiphase eutectic alloy will have greater corrosion penetration than the homogeneous baseline.
A compositionally matched homogeneous single-phase alloy lacks the microstructural heterogeneity required to form localized phase-scale galvanic cells.
The proposed mechanism applies nominally from 150 to 250 °C in a chloride-containing medium under simultaneous sliding wear and corrosion.
The magnitude of synergistic acceleration depends on phase distribution, phase potentials, mechanical load, temperature, and corrosive conditions.
